Based on the healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that there is a lack of empirical evidence supporting the existence of an "early adopter" of drugs. In fact, several studies suggest that physicians' adoption of new drugs can be influenced by various factors beyond personal traits, such as type of drug, physician experience, and institutional pressures.

While some studies have reported correlations between early exposure to certain medications and adverse outcomes later in life (e.g., pregnancy-related complications), these findings are not robust or consistent across all research. In the case of prenatal exposure to cigarettes and violence, for example, one study found no association with self-reported delinquent behaviors during early adolescence.

Moreover, a review of medical literature suggests that current evidence does not support the idea that specialty pharmaceuticals provide good healthcare value when used in targeted patient populations.

Therefore, it is unlikely that an "early adopter" of drugs exists, and further research is needed to fully understand the factors influencing physicians' adoption of new medications.
